title: Windows Update Success Recency and Repeated Installation Failures
exclusions: Measures only recency of Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient event 19 and repeated event 20 records for explicitly inventoried Windows hosts. It does not prove that the latest required monthly quality update, feature update, servicing-stack update, Defender intelligence, driver, Microsoft Store package, or application update is installed; event 19 can describe different update classes. It does not establish Intune, Windows Autopatch, WSUS, Configuration Manager, vulnerability-management, contractual, or regulatory compliance. Missing event history may mean stale collection rather than missing patches. The 30-day recency objective, three failures in 24 hours, expected-host lookup, schedule, and exceptions are local policy choices, not Microsoft or Splunk defaults. This UC does not install, approve, decline, pause, roll back, or reboot for updates.
evidence: After deployment, retain the `windows_update_event_health` saved-search definition, ACL, daily schedule, dispatch history, and per-host rows; effective WindowsUpdateClient Operational input and add-on configuration; `windows_update_expected_hosts.csv` and `windows_update_exceptions.csv` revisions with approvals and expiry; raw event-19/20 drilldowns; field/source-health checks; dashboard exports; alert dispositions; and dated boundary, absence, exception, and recovery tests. Evidence demonstrates event-history recency or repeated failures under a local policy. It is not an update-compliance attestation. This documentation-only review created no Windows update, event, search, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Fix dispatch time at 2026-07-28T06:00:00Z and put `host=win-lab-01, asset_id=A-1001, owner=endpoint-lab, update_ring=lab, monitor_from=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z, monitor_until=` in `windows_update_expected_hosts.csv`. Variant A indexes one valid provider event 19 at exactly 2026-06-27T05:59:59Z and no later success; expect one `stale_or_missing_success` row because recency is greater than 30 times 86,400 seconds. Variant B indexes a recent event 19 plus three provider event 20 records in the preceding 24 hours; expect one `repeated_installation_failure` row with `failure_events_24h=3`. Assert host, asset, owner, ring, epoch, age, reason, and UC ID.
controlTest.negativeScenario: With the same fixed dispatch and inventory, run independent variants and expect zero rows: event 19 exactly 30 days old with fewer than three event-20 records in 24 hours; a recent event 19 plus exactly two event-20 records; three event-20 records where one is 24 hours and one second old; records with the wrong provider, channel source, source type, or event ID; and a host whose `monitor_from` is in the future or `monitor_until` has passed. A matching active row in `windows_update_exceptions.csv` may suppress delivery only after a base finding exists; an expired row must not. A host with no event 19 in 35 days must produce a stale/missing row, while absence of all WindowsUpdateClient events must also produce an independent source-health finding.

dataSources: The Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) collects `[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational]` in classic or XML form. Search `source=WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational, sourcetype=WinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational, sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Required event fields are `_time, host, source, sourcetype, SourceName, EventCode, Message`; event 19 is installation success and event 20 is installation failure. Deployment-owned `windows_update_expected_hosts.csv` supplies `host, asset_id, owner, update_ring, monitor_from, monitor_until`; `windows_update_exceptions.csv` supplies exact-host expiry and approval. `index=windows` is an explicit local routing choice, not an add-on default.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for WindowsUpdateClient Operational collection. A deployment-owned search app supplies expected-host and exception lookups, source-health logic, saved search, dashboard, and tests; no premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=windows (source="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational") (sourcetype=WinEventLog OR sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog) SourceName="Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient" EventCode IN (19,20) earliest=-35d
| eval host=lower(host), success_epoch=if(EventCode=19,_time,null()), failure_epoch=if(EventCode=20,_time,null()), recent_failure=if(EventCode=20 AND _time>=relative_time(now(),"-24h"),1,0)
| stats max(success_epoch) AS last_success_epoch max(failure_epoch) AS last_failure_epoch sum(recent_failure) AS failure_events_24h latest(_time) AS last_update_event_epoch by host
| append [| inputlookup windows_update_expected_hosts.csv | eval host=lower(host), monitor_from_epoch=strptime(monitor_from,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), monitor_until_epoch=if(len(monitor_until)>0,strptime(monitor_until,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),null()), expected=if(monitor_from_epoch<=now() AND (isnull(monitor_until_epoch) OR monitor_until_epoch>now()),1,0) | where expected=1 | fields host asset_id owner update_ring expected]
| stats max(last_success_epoch) AS last_success_epoch max(last_failure_epoch) AS last_failure_epoch sum(failure_events_24h) AS failure_events_24h max(last_update_event_epoch) AS last_update_event_epoch max(expected) AS expected values(asset_id) AS asset_id values(owner) AS owner values(update_ring) AS update_ring by host
| where expected=1
| eval days_since_success=if(isnull(last_success_epoch),null(),floor((now()-last_success_epoch)/86400)), stale_or_missing_success=if(isnull(last_success_epoch) OR (now()-last_success_epoch)>2592000,1,0), repeated_installation_failure=if(failure_events_24h>=3,1,0), finding_reason=case(stale_or_missing_success=1 AND repeated_installation_failure=1,"stale_or_missing_success;repeated_installation_failure",stale_or_missing_success=1,"stale_or_missing_success",repeated_installation_failure=1,"repeated_installation_failure")
| where stale_or_missing_success=1 OR repeated_installation_failure=1
| lookup windows_update_exceptions.csv host OUTPUT exception_until reason AS exception_reason ticket
| eval exception_until_epoch=if(match(exception_until,"^\d+$"),tonumber(exception_until),strptime(exception_until,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")), exception_active=if(isnotnull(exception_until_epoch) AND exception_until_epoch>now(),1,0)
| where exception_active=0
| eval use_case_id="UC-1.2.127"
| convert ctime(last_success_epoch) ctime(last_failure_epoch) ctime(last_update_event_epoch)
| table host asset_id owner update_ring finding_reason days_since_success failure_events_24h last_success_epoch last_failure_epoch last_update_event_epoch use_case_id
| sort 0 -days_since_success -failure_events_24h host
description: Reports results once daily by evaluating each active host in the governed Windows inventory. A row is emitted when no event-19 installation success exists within the preceding 30 times 86,400 seconds, or when at least three event-20 installation failures occurred during the preceding 24 hours; each result remains one host with owner and update-ring context.
value: The signal finds broken update workflows and silent telemetry before they become a long-lived exposure or missed maintenance objective. It gives endpoint teams a bounded queue for troubleshooting while preventing a convenient event-history proxy from being represented as proof that required security updates are installed.
implementation: Collect the WindowsUpdateClient Operational channel with the supported Windows add-on, govern an expected-host inventory, and validate event 19/20 provider semantics and deployed field extraction. Run the search daily with a 35-day event history. Treat more than 30 days since success and at least three failures in 24 hours as local starting objectives, tune by update ring, and route findings to endpoint operations. Use Intune, Autopatch, WSUS, Configuration Manager, or another authoritative update-state product for actual patch compliance.
visualization: Endpoint-operations dashboard with source-health and inventory-coverage tiles, a table of governed hosts by finding reason and update ring, a histogram of days since last event-19 success, a 30-day event-20 trend, and drilldowns to raw update titles/error codes and the authoritative update-management console. Label all panels “event history, not patch-compliance proof.”

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Microsoft Intune or Windows Autopatch deployment pause** — a device can intentionally remain behind while its governed quality-update ring is paused. Confirm the device, ring, pause owner, and end time in the Intune admin center; add an exact-host exception in `windows_update_exceptions.csv` with ticket and `exception_until` no later than the approved pause end.

2. **Configuration Manager or WSUS staged pilot ring** — lab/pilot devices may have a monthly cadence longer than the initial 30-day objective. Distinguish them with `update_ring` and the approved deployment schedule; encode a ring-specific policy or a bounded exact-host exception rather than globally increasing the threshold.

3. **Microsoft Store or driver update event-20 burst** — three failures may concern an application or driver rather than the operating-system quality update. Inspect raw event titles/error codes and the update-management console; suppress only the exact host during an approved remediation window, while preserving the base finding and separate security-update state.

4. **Retired, reimaged, or renamed device in CMDB/Intune** — stale inventory creates a missing-success row for an asset that should no longer be monitored. Verify serial/device identity and retirement or rename record; close or version the row in `windows_update_expected_hosts.csv` with `monitor_until`, never use a permanent wildcard exception.

5. **WindowsUpdateClient channel or forwarder outage** — missing event 19 can be collection failure rather than patch failure. Compare last event of any ID, forwarder heartbeat, and Event Viewer **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > WindowsUpdateClient > Operational**. Repair collection and keep the source-health alert open; do not mark the host current.

6. **Offline disaster-recovery image or powered-down seasonal host** — a governed cold standby can legitimately have no recent event while offline. Confirm documented activation/patch procedure and owner; use a time-bound lifecycle exception and require update-state verification before service activation.

Only `windows_update_exceptions.csv` with exact `host,exception_until,reason,ticket,owner` may suppress delivery after the base row is produced. Expired or malformed entries, unknown hosts, and source-health failures remain visible.

Implement suppression through a governed post-result lookup table; retain the unsuppressed base result and require the exact keys and finite expiry described above.
reviewer: documentation-only Cursor AI editorial review against Microsoft WindowsUpdateClient event-19/event-20 examples, Windows Update logging, Intune quality-update reporting, and Splunk Windows Event Log/add-on/scheduled-alert documentation; channel enablement, event generation, field extraction, inventory, fixtures, SPL, thresholds, source health, authoritative compliance comparison, alert delivery, update state, versions, and production response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Splunk/endpoint/update-management/SME signed
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact claim

Assign endpoint/update-management, Windows platform, vulnerability, asset/CMDB, Splunk data, Splunk content, service-desk, and security owners. Use supported Windows endpoints, Universal Forwarders, and a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) release qualified in the deployment. This editorial review did not run any version combination, so no `splunkVersions` field is asserted. The forwarder identity needs read access to the WindowsUpdateClient Operational channel and ordinary encrypted forwarding; it does not need update-approval, installation, registry-write, reboot, or local-administrator rights merely for collection. The search role needs the chosen index, lookup read access, and schedule permission. Restrict expected-host and exception writes to governed owners.

Define the result precisely. Microsoft demonstrates WindowsUpdateClient event 19 as “Installation Successful” and event 20 as “Installation Failure.” This UC uses those records only to measure event-history recency and repeated failures. A recent event 19 does not identify whether every required update is present, and an old event 19 can occur on a device that correctly had no applicable installation. Microsoft Intune and Windows Autopatch expose device-level quality-update status, version/build, readiness, and alerts; WSUS or Configuration Manager may be the local authority elsewhere. Compare to that authority and never publish this search as “percent compliant.”

The initial objectives are: more than 2,592,000 seconds (30 times 86,400) since the latest event 19, or at least three event 20 records in the preceding 86,400 seconds. Exactly 30 days is healthy for the recency branch; exactly three failures fires. These are local operational values. Record approved values by update ring and review them after servicing-cadence changes. The 35-day raw search is a five-day observation buffer; a host with no event 19 in that range remains a missing-success finding through the inventory append.

## Step 1 — Configure collection and governed inventory

Deploy `Splunk_TA_windows` following its supported topology. Enable `[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational]` and route it to the deployment's Windows index. The SPL's `index=windows` is an explicit local choice. Classic collection is expected as `source=WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational, sourcetype=WinEventLog`; XML is expected as `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational, sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Verify these values instead of inventing a channel-specific sourcetype. If `renderXml=1` and input filtering is added, Splunk requires `$XmlRegex` filtering.

Inspect 24 hours of events and validate `_time, host, source, sourcetype, SourceName, EventCode, Message`. Provider must be `Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient`. Confirm event 19 and 20 semantics on the deployed Windows builds in Event Viewer at **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > WindowsUpdateClient > Operational**. Preserve raw XML fields and rendered message for drilldown, but do not make update-title/error-code extraction part of the primary threshold until the field names are observed and version-qualified.

Create `windows_update_expected_hosts.csv` with `host,asset_id,owner,update_ring,monitor_from,monitor_until`. Use lowercase canonical host keys, stable asset IDs, UTC timestamps, one active row per monitored host, and an explicit end when retired. Reconcile daily with the authoritative endpoint inventory. Duplicate keys, missing owners/rings, malformed dates, future monitor dates, and vanished hosts are data-quality findings. The search app also contains `windows_update_exceptions.csv` with `host,exception_until,reason,ticket,owner`; forbid wildcard-only keys and permanent expiry.

Build an independent source-health search from all WindowsUpdateClient event IDs plus Universal Forwarder heartbeat. Compare expected active hosts with latest event and forwarding time. Event 19 can legitimately be infrequent, so lack of event 19 alone is not enough to call the feed broken. Lack of all channel events, forwarder heartbeat, or expected Windows telemetry is source-health evidence and must not be converted to “not patched.”

## Step 2 — Create and schedule the search

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_update_event_health`. The first stage reads only provider event 19 and 20 for 35 days. It calculates event-19 success epochs, event-20 failure epochs, and event-20 records inside the latest rolling 24 hours. `stats` first produces one row per observed host. `append` adds every active governed host, including those absent from event data. The second `stats` joins those rows by canonical host without a subsearch cardinality join. Only expected active hosts continue.

The recency branch compares dispatch `now()` with the latest success epoch using seconds, avoiding rounded-day ambiguity. The failure branch is `>=3` in rolling 24 hours. The lookup is applied after the base finding so exceptions suppress delivery, not measurement. Output remains one host with asset, owner, ring, reason, age, failure count, source times, and UC ID. Do not add `latest(Status)`; a later unrelated success must not erase counted failures, and a failure must not overwrite success recency.

Schedule once daily at a documented low-contention time such as `15 6 * * *`. Splunk Cloud uses UTC for cron; Splunk Enterprise uses the search-head timezone, so record the effective zone. Trigger per result and throttle by host for 24 hours. A changed reason or worsening age remains visible on the dashboard even if notification is throttled. Set scheduler priority/capacity appropriate to fleet size and monitor skipped searches. Never invoke update installation or reboot directly from this alert.

## Step 3 — Validate boundaries, absence, and source truth

Run every `controlTest` fixture in an isolated index with fixed dispatch epoch. Test event 19 at 30 days, 30 days plus one second, and no event; event 20 at counts two and three; a third failure exactly 24 hours old and one second outside; wrong provider/source/source type/event ID; lowercase/uppercase host normalization; active/future/retired inventory; duplicate inventory; active/expired/malformed exception; event-only host absent from inventory; and inventory-only host absent from events. Assert output columns and one row per host.

On two nonproduction hosts, compare raw event time, provider, ID, computer, update title, and error code with Event Viewer. In the authoritative update console, compare current quality update/build and policy status at the same UTC observation time. Expected mismatches prove the limitation: an event-19 record can represent a driver or application update, and a device can have no recent install because no update was applicable. Record those cases rather than tuning the claim away.

Run `timechart span=1h count by host` over seven days for the channel, inspect `_indextime-_time`, test delayed and out-of-order events, and compare active inventory count with result/source-health coverage. Validate scheduler dispatch, lookup replication, role ACL, alert payload, throttle, dashboard labels, and incident routing. Keep `status=draft` until accountable owners accept tested Windows/add-on/Splunk versions, fields, inventory, thresholds by ring, source-health behavior, authoritative-console comparison, fixtures, alert delivery, exceptions, and response.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response and evidence

Dashboard order: expected-host/source-health coverage; findings by reason and ring; days-since-success histogram; 24-hour failure counts; 30-day raw event trend; exception-expiry table; and drilldown to raw events and authoritative update console. Never label an event-based ratio “compliance.” Restrict raw messages if usernames or device data require it. Retain versioned searches/lookups, dispatch records, field checks, console comparisons, test results, alerts, and dispositions under operational policy.

Responder sequence: (1) verify expected inventory identity, owner, ring, source health, extraction, dispatch epoch, lookup expiry, and exact boundary; (2) inspect raw event 19/20 titles and error codes; (3) open Intune/Autopatch, WSUS, Configuration Manager, or the approved update authority and determine current build, required update, deployment state, pause, deadline, and error; (4) check WindowsUpdateClient Operational and Microsoft-documented Windows Update logs, including CBS/ETW as appropriate; (5) correlate proxy, Delivery Optimization, disk, servicing-stack, policy, reboot, and maintenance context; (6) apply the update-management runbook under change control; (7) verify authoritative current state and a new valid success/failure disposition; and (8) require a healthy source plus a nonfinding search before closure. Event 19 by itself is not closure proof.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot without overclaiming

- **Expected host has no row before filtering:** test `inputlookup windows_update_expected_hosts.csv`, date parsing, lowercase key, search-head lookup replication, and role permissions. Inventory-only active hosts must survive `append`.
- **All hosts show missing success:** confirm index routing, exact channel source, `SourceName`, sourcetype, 35-day retention, search-role access, and event availability on the endpoint. Do not raise the threshold to hide a feed outage.
- **Event Viewer has records but Splunk does not:** inspect the exact input stanza, channel enabled state, forwarder/deployment logs, XML/classic mode, index routing, queue state, and add-on knowledge placement.
- **Failure count seems high:** check duplicate local plus Windows Event Forwarding collection, repeated retry events for one update, update class/title, and event record identity. Repair duplicates; retain repeated genuine attempts because the branch intentionally counts event records, not unique updates.
- **Recent success is an application/driver update:** expected limitation. Consult the authoritative quality-update report and avoid calling the host patched. A later enhancement may version-qualify title/update-ID extraction.
- **Console and event disagree:** align device identity, tenant/site, ring, UTC observation time, scan/report latency, update class, build, and supersedence. Preserve both sources and let the authoritative platform determine compliance.
- **Host renamed or reimaged:** version the inventory identity and monitor dates; do not merge unrelated history solely by reused hostname.
- **Exception remains active too long:** verify UTC parsing, ticket, owner, reason, and expiry governance. Remove malformed/permanent entries and rerun the base search.
- **Scheduled search skips:** inspect scheduler workload and runtime, distribute cron, reduce retained raw payload, and monitor skipped-search telemetry. Never interpret a skipped dispatch as healthy.
- **Remediation needs deeper logs:** follow Microsoft's Windows Update log guidance and generate readable ETW logs under approved support procedures; collecting diagnostics is separate from this event-history detector.
grandmaExplanation: We check whether each Windows computer has recently reported a successful update and whether update attempts keep failing. This is an early warning for the support team, not proof that every required patch is installed.
